name: Appeal to motive
statement: Pointing at what a speaker stands to gain is treated as a refutation, and disclosing the interest can make the advice worse rather than the audience wiser.
meaning: The move runs from a fact about the speaker to a verdict on the claim. Someone benefits if a proposition is believed, therefore the proposition is not to be believed. Textbooks list it as a fallacy because an interested speaker can still be right, and the Stanford Encyclopedia's example is the pollution study produced by industrialists, which may be sound however self-serving it looks. Two questions hide inside that verdict and pull in different directions. The first is evidential: does knowing who paid predict what the study found. The answer for industry-sponsored drug and device trials is yes, by a measured amount. The second is practical: given that it predicts something, do audiences discount by the right amount when the interest is put in front of them. The experimental answer is that they do not, and that telling them can leave them worse off than not telling them. The atlas covers the personal attack under ad hominem, dismissal by origin under genetic fallacy, and the persuasion side of source credibility under source bias. This entry takes the interest itself.

origin.note: Section 3 of the chapter on Vituperative Personalities, ad odium, is headed 'Imputation of bad motive' and sits at page 133 of the 1824 Hunt edition. Bentham gives two grounds for calling it weak: 'because motives are hidden in the human breast', and 'because, if the measure is beneficial, it would be absurd to reject it on account of the motives of its author'. He then adds a utilitarian objection the retellings drop, that there is no class of motive to which the epithet bad can properly be applied, since a motive is the expectation of pleasure or of exemption from pain and neither is bad in itself. The cluster's common character, he writes, is 'the endeavour to draw aside attention from the measure to the man'. The name 'appeal to motive' is not Bentham's and was not traced to any document read here. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy lists the move as 'Faulty Motives', a kind of ad hominem fallacy, with a councilman who stands to gain from the convention centre he argues for.

evidence:
Interest predicts conclusion, and the size is known for one case. Lundh and colleagues' Cochrane methodology review pooled 75 papers comparing industry-sponsored drug and device studies with studies funded otherwise. Industry-sponsored studies more often had favourable efficacy results, RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.37, from 25 papers, and more often had favourable conclusions, RR 1.34, 95% CI 1.19 to 1.51, from 29 papers. They agreed less often with their own results, RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.98, from six papers. Standard risk-of-bias assessment did not explain the association, and the review's authors call it an industry bias. That is the same review quoted in this atlas under genetic fallacy, and it was read again here.

The move persuades. Barnes and colleagues gave participants science claims attributed to named researchers, each followed by one of six kinds of extra information, and scored attitude as a difference from the same claim presented alone. Being told the researcher had been a paid consultant for the company whose product was at issue moved attitude by -.59 in 439 undergraduates, t(438) = 8.67, d = .41, and by -.83 in 199 adults from a national panel, t(198) = 8.15, d = .58. In both experiments that condition did not differ from being told the study lacked a control group, -.63 and -.57. The two attacks on competence did nothing: a doctorate from a low-standard institution gave -.07 twice, and a reputation for sloppiness gave -.15 and -.12, neither surviving the Bonferroni-corrected alpha of .008. Attacking motive worked, and attacking ability did not.

The move is also common in at least one place it has been counted. Wolfe, Sharp and Lipsky examined 22 antivaccination websites found in late 2000 and coded 11 content claims. Ninety-one percent asserted that vaccination policy is motivated by profit, behind only the claims that vaccines cause idiopathic illness, at 100%, that they erode immunity, at 95%, and that adverse reactions are underreported, also at 95%. Twenty-two sites is a small base and the coding is two decades old.

What happens when the interest is disclosed is the part that surprises. Cain, Loewenstein and Moore paired 126 advisors with 135 estimators, who guessed the sale prices of four real houses from information packets while the advisor held extra information on comparable sales and tax assessments. Advisors were paid either for their estimator's accuracy or for how high the estimate came out, and that incentive was either disclosed on the advisor's report in the advisor's handwriting or not mentioned. Conflicted advisors inflated their suggestions above their own private estimates by $31,351 without disclosure and by $51,562 with it, t(122) = 2.24, p < .05. Mean suggestions were $236,138 undisclosed against $255,394 disclosed, t(118) = 2.5, p < .05, against roughly $204,000 in both unconflicted conditions. Estimators did discount more when told, $25,609 against $11,216, but only marginally, t(75) = 1.81, p = .07, and not enough. Their estimates came out $8,000 higher with disclosure than without, which was not significant, t(131) = 1.21, p = .23. The payoffs settled it. Estimators earned $1.86 in each unconflicted condition, $1.37 facing an undisclosed conflict and $0.87 facing a disclosed one, t(131) = 2.2, p < .05. Advisors earned $2.67 and $2.98. Two rounds of feedback on actual sale prices did not remove the effect.

replication.headline: A direct replication reproduced the finding that disclosure makes advisors more biased and, like the original, found little effect on advisees. An independent experiment in a different design found disclosure changed nothing at all, and the same author reports the sign reversing where professional norms put the client first.
replication.detail: Sah repeated the main study of Cain, Loewenstein and Moore on advisors, with slight changes for advisees, and reports replicating the original finding that advisors give more biased advice with disclosure than without when recommending house sale prices to advisees who hold less information. Like the original, she found little or no support for effects on advisees, whether higher estimates, worse accuracy or more discounting. A meta-analysis across the original study and the replication put advisees financially worse off with disclosure than without. The article was not obtained beyond its published abstract, so no figure from it appears above. Her stated reason for running it was that her own earlier experiments had found advisors giving less biased advice with disclosure in some settings, which is a contradiction rather than a confirmation. Ismayilov and Potters ran a sender-receiver game in which the receiver either did or did not see the sender's payoffs. Disclosure raised the deception rate by 9 percentage points under low incentives and 2 under high, neither significant, p = 0.56 and p = 0.86 by two-tailed chi-square, on 34 senders without disclosure and 61 with. Their conclusion is that disclosure neither hurts nor helps, which they call bad news for disclosure policy and good news against the backfire result. The three studies do not sit in one direction, and the design differs at every point that might matter: real houses against abstract payoffs, handwritten disclosure against a payoff table, four rounds against two.

study.cite: Sah, S. (2019). Understanding the (perverse) effects of disclosing conflicts of interest: A direct replication study. Journal of Economic Psychology, 75, 102118.

limits:
No meta-analysis of disclosure experiments was located. Searches ran over Crossref by bibliographic query, Europe PMC, and general web search, and returned a 2024 meta-analysis of advice weighting in the judge-advisor paradigm, which is a different question and is not used here.

Sah's replication is closed access and was not obtained. Everything attributed to it comes from the abstract as printed on the publisher's record, and no number from it is quoted. Her earlier paper on professional norms, in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, is named only because the replication's abstract cites it as the contradiction that prompted the study; the abstract dates it 2018 and the journal record dates it 2019, and neither the paper nor the reason for the discrepancy was checked.

Ismayilov and Potters were read as the 2012 Netspar working paper, not as the 2013 article in the Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization. The figures above are the working paper's and may differ from the published version. Their receiver-side percentages are reported in a sentence whose ordering is ambiguous about which treatment each figure belongs to, so they are left out.

The first Cain, Loewenstein and Moore study, the coin-jar experiment published in the Journal of Legal Studies in 2005, was not obtained. Its design is described above only as the later paper describes it, and no figure from it appears. The copy of the 2011 article read here is the authors' PDF hosted by Carnegie Mellon; the DOI printed in its footer, 10.1086/655862, resolves at Crossref to a different article by different authors, and the correct DOI is the one cited below.

Douglas Walton's treatment of the bias and circumstantial subtypes of the ad hominem, and of bias as a critical question rather than an automatic fallacy, could not be read. His 1998 book and his 2001 and 2004 papers in Argumentation were sought at the publisher, at his own site and at two open repositories, and none returned a document. Nothing is attributed to him here.

The randomised trials asking whether doctors discount a study for its disclosed industry funding sit in this atlas under genetic fallacy, which records that one found a discount and two later ones found none. They are not repeated here.

Bentham's page numbers are from the 1824 Hunt edition, read in two independent scans. The Stanford Encyclopedia cites the same passage at page 83, which is some other edition's pagination, and the discrepancy was not resolved.
misreadings:
The commonest error is that motive is irrelevant to truth. Bentham himself did not hold that. Ninety pages before the fallacy he sets out what sinister interest does to the weight of an opinion, and says that where the interest and the opinion point the same way the probative force is not merely zero but negative. He then draws the asymmetry that the modern literature keeps rediscovering: 'In a man's own favour his own testimony is the weakest, in his disfavour, the strongest, evidence.' Sponsorship predicts the result, RR 1.27 for favourable efficacy findings, so weighing it is not irrelevance.

The mirror error is treating the prediction as a verdict. RR 1.27 is a statement about a population of studies. It licenses a discount on an industry-funded finding; it does not license the conclusion that this finding is wrong. The same review found no difference between sponsored and unsponsored studies in sequence generation, allocation concealment, follow-up or selective outcome reporting, and found sponsored studies at low risk of bias from blinding more often, RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.50, from 13 papers.

Calling something a fallacy is not calling it ineffective. Barnes's paid-consultant condition moved attitudes as far as being told the study lacked a control group, in both a student sample and an adult panel, while two attacks on the researcher's competence moved nothing.

Disclosure is read as the remedy, and the strongest experimental result in this literature is that it can be the opposite. In Cain's house study the estimators who were told earned less than half what the unconflicted estimators earned, and less than the estimators facing a hidden conflict, because advisors who had disclosed felt free to exaggerate further and advisors' extra bias outran the discount. Sah's replication reproduced the advisor half of that and, pooling both studies, the advisee half.

The backfire result is also quoted more confidently than it holds. Neither the original nor the replication found the advisee effects the model predicts, an independent experiment found nothing in either direction, and the same author reports the effect reversing where the advisor's profession expects clients to come first.

sources.text: Bentham, J. (1824). The Book of Fallacies: From Unfinished Papers of Jeremy Bentham. By a Friend. London: John and H. L. Hunt. 'Sect. 3. Imputation of bad motive' at pages 133-134, the cluster's common character at pages 127-129, and the sinister-interest passage at pages 40-41. Read in the Internet Archive scan of the 1824 edition and checked again against an independent transcription of the same edition.

Bentham, J. (1824). The Book of Fallacies. Transcription of the John and H. L. Hunt edition in the Digital Library of Liberty and Power, with the original page numbers. The second reading of every Bentham passage quoted here.

Cain, D. M., Loewenstein, G., & Moore, D. A. (2011). When Sunlight Fails to Disinfect: Understanding the Perverse Effects of Disclosing Conflicts of Interest. Journal of Consumer Research, 37(5), 836-857. Study 3 read in full from the authors' PDF hosted by Carnegie Mellon; every figure taken from the results text and checked against tables 1, 2 and 3.

Sah, S. (2019). Understanding the (perverse) effects of disclosing conflicts of interest: A direct replication study. Journal of Economic Psychology, 75, 102118. Closed access on this pass; described here from the published abstract, and no figure from it is quoted.

Ismayilov, H., & Potters, J. (2013). Disclosing advisor's interests neither hurts nor helps. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, 93, 314-320. Read as the 2012 Netspar discussion paper 09/2012-058, which is the source of the deception rates and sample sizes above.

Lundh, A., Lexchin, J., Mintzes, B., Schroll, J. B., & Bero, L. (2017). Industry sponsorship and research outcome. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MR000033.pub3. The pooled risk ratios were read in the Europe PMC record of the review.

Barnes, R. M., Johnston, H. M., MacKenzie, N., Tobin, S. J., & Taglang, C. M. (2018). The effect of ad hominem attacks on the evaluation of claims promoted by scientists. PLOS ONE, 13(1), e0192025. Read as the Europe PMC full-text XML; the conflict-of-interest figures come from tables 2 and 3.

Wolfe, R. M., Sharp, L. K., & Lipsky, M. S. (2002). Content and design attributes of antivaccination web sites. JAMA, 287(24), 3245-3248. The 91% and the other content-claim percentages were read in the Europe PMC record of the abstract.

Hansen, H. (2024). Fallacies. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, substantive revision 30 August 2024. Source for the circumstantial ad hominem and the industrialists' pollution study, and for Bentham's vituperative fallacies. Fetched twice.

Dowden, B. Fallacies. Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Fetched in full and searched; the entry 'Faulty Motives' and its convention-centre example were read there, and the string 'appeal to motive' does not appear on that page.

Cain, D. M., Loewenstein, G., & Moore, D. A. (2005). The Dirt on Coming Clean: Perverse Effects of Disclosing Conflicts of Interest. The Journal of Legal Studies, 34(1), 1-25. The coin-jar precursor to the house study. Not obtained; named here because the 2011 paper describes it and lists its shortcomings, and no figure from it is quoted.

Sah, S. (2019). Conflict of interest disclosure as a reminder of professional norms: Clients first! Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 154, 62-79. Named because the replication's abstract cites it as the finding that contradicts the backfire result; not obtained, and its year is given as 2018 in that abstract.

Walton, D. N. (2001). Searching for the Roots of the Circumstantial Ad Hominem. Argumentation, 15(2), 207-221. Sought at the publisher and at two repositories and not obtained. Listed to record where the search for the standard treatment of bias as a critical question looked.
